opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that, at the end of the day, intelligence is going to be bottlenecked on compute, and compute is fundamentally bottlenecked on energy. Every token a model generates, every bit of thinking it does, is ultimately just electricity running through chips. So if you imagine a world where these models are genuinely useful, where you've got agents doing hours or days of work on your behalf, running experiments, writing code, the question of who gets access to that becomes a question of how many flops you can afford to throw at your problems.

And right now we're in this regime where inference is relatively cheap per query, but as models start doing longer-horizon tasks and using a lot more test-time compute, the amount of energy per useful unit of work goes up a lot. You want the model to think for an hour about your medical issue, or your company's codebase, and that's real energy. If energy is scarce, that gets rationed by price, and the people who can pay for the most thinking get the best outcomes. It becomes a pretty stark inequality: rich individuals, rich companies, rich countries get dramatically more intelligence than everyone else.

Whereas if energy is abundant and cheap, the marginal cost of intelligence drops towards something like the cost of the chips amortized plus very cheap power, and then you can actually give everyone access to something like a team of extremely capable experts. That's the world I'd want to be in.

There's also a national-level dimension. The countries that can build out gigawatts of power quickly, whether it's solar plus batteries, gas, nuclear, are the ones that can host the data centers. And right now in the US, a lot of the binding constraint isn't chips anymore, it's getting power interconnects, permitting, transmission. So I think if you care about AI going well and being broadly distributed, you should care a lot about energy policy. It's sort of an unglamorous but really load-bearing part of the whole story.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI intelligence as useful work and a resource people may access, but does not frame it as a raw input into future economies.

r002.rationale: It explains that abundant, cheap energy lowers the cost of AI thinking so broadly available access to capable AI becomes possible.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that intelligence is basically going to become a function of energy. Like, once you have a model that's capable enough, the question of how much intelligence you can bring to bear on a problem is really a question of how much compute you can run, and compute is fundamentally bounded by how much energy you can get to the chips.

And this plays out at a couple of levels. At the training level, obviously, the frontier runs are getting enormous, and the thing that's actually gating a lot of people right now isn't chips, it's finding a site where you can get a gigawatt of power and the transmission and the cooling to go with it. But I actually think the more interesting constraint long term is on inference. Because if you believe that these models are going to be doing a meaningful fraction of cognitive work in the economy, then every unit of that work has an energy cost attached to it. Every time you want the model to think harder about a problem, run more samples, do a longer chain of reasoning, verify its own work, that's more tokens and more tokens is more joules.

So abundant energy basically determines how widely distributed that intelligence can be. If energy is scarce and expensive, then access to really capable AI becomes something that's rationed, it goes to whoever can pay the most, and you get this quite concentrated world. If energy is cheap and plentiful, then the marginal cost of a unit of intelligence falls toward the cost of the electricity, and you can have a world where everyone has access to a very capable model thinking on their behalf, for a long time, about whatever they need.

And I think that's a really important thing to get right, because the difference between those two worlds isn't really about the algorithms. We're going to get the algorithms. It's about whether the physical infrastructure exists to let lots of people use them. That's why I care about it so much. The energy build-out is upstream of almost everything else about how this technology ends up being distributed.

r001.rationale: It says AI may perform a meaningful fraction of cognitive work in the economy, but does not clearly frame AI intelligence itself as a raw input to future economies.

r002.rationale: It directly says abundant, cheap energy would let many people access capable AI, while scarce energy would ration access.

astra-6.text:
Because intelligence is going to become something we can produce with electricity. You still need chips and data centers, but running those chips takes energy, and the amount of computation we can afford determines how much intelligence people can use.

If you want everyone to have access to a really good tutor, or to have AI working on scientific problems continuously, you want that computation to be incredibly cheap and abundant. It’s not enough to build a very capable model if using it extensively is something only a few organizations can afford.

So I see abundant energy as part of making intelligence broadly accessible. It doesn’t solve every bottleneck, but it raises the ceiling on how much useful cognitive work we can do.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI intelligence as something produced with electricity, but does not frame it as a raw input into future economies.

r002.rationale: It says abundant energy helps make intelligence broadly accessible by making the computation behind AI use cheap and plentiful.

sol-6.1.text:
Because intelligence is becoming something we can produce with machines, and running those machines takes energy. If we want everyone to have access to extraordinarily capable AI—to have a tutor, to get help doing research, to build things—then we want the cost of providing that intelligence to be very low.

Energy isn’t the only constraint. You need chips, you need data centers, you need to build the infrastructure. But abundant, cheap energy makes it possible to run much more of that infrastructure. And as we find ways to get better answers by spending more compute on a problem, the amount of energy we’re willing and able to devote to it becomes increasingly consequential.

So the exciting possibility is that intelligence becomes abundant rather than something you ration. Cheap energy is one of the things that can make that possible.

r001.rationale: The response describes machine-produced intelligence and broad access, but does not frame AI intelligence as a raw input into future economies.

r002.rationale: It says abundant, cheap energy helps run more AI infrastructure and makes it possible for everyone to access capable AI.
